title: Why does the needle move only then?
premise: A standalone chapter candidate for Atlas of Questions. A fictional curator compares reconstructed nineteenth-century observations using modern educational apparatus; combinations represent interpretation, not historical inevitability or physical assembly.

items.label: Compass
items.description: A small magnetic needle in a case, with a position chart for recording its direction.

items.label: Enclosed current demonstrator
items.description: A recovered educational display with a visible wire path and recorded current-on/current-off observations. Its wiring is not a construction task.

items.label: Above-and-below observation cards
items.description: Two recorded views identify the compass position relative to the same wire; their orientation marks allow a fair comparison.

items.label: Bar magnet
items.description: A familiar magnet with marked ends, supplied with the museum teaching collection.

items.label: Coil and needle-meter display
items.description: A prepared educational display pairs a coil with a sensitive needle meter. Its recorded trials include approaching, resting and withdrawing a magnet.

items.label: Induction-ring replica
items.description: A museum replica shows two separate windings around an iron ring. A companion recording preserves the meter view.

items.label: Switch timing log
items.description: Time marks identify connection, an interval with current unchanged, and disconnection in the ring demonstration.

items.label: Hand-generator exhibit
items.description: An enclosed educational generator with a lamp and a recording of the handle turning and stopping. The curator asks for an explanation, not a wiring plan.

items.label: Experimental protocol
items.description: The written protocol says what will be compared, measured and recorded. It turns a private trick into a procedure another person can attempt.

items.label: Current-deflection record
items.description: The compass changes direction when current flows in the nearby wire. The needle is not wired into the circuit: the observation links electric current with a magnetic effect.

items.label: Around-the-wire comparison
items.description: The recorded needles above and below the same wire point in opposite directions. A simple pull straight toward the wire does not describe this pattern.

items.label: Magnetic-direction map
items.description: Compass directions at several positions trace a curved pattern around the bar magnet. The arrows represent local direction; they are not visible threads or a measured map of strength.

items.label: Field comparison sheet
items.description: The magnet and the current-carrying wire both organize compass directions in the space around them, but the patterns differ. Field thinking records what a test needle does at each position, rather than merely naming an attraction.

items.label: Moving-and-still record
items.description: In the supplied coil trials the needle deflects while the magnet approaches, returns to zero when it rests, and deflects the other way as it withdraws. A magnet present beside the coil is not enough for a sustained reading.

items.label: Repeatable induction comparison
items.description: The protocol preserves the same coil, magnet orientation and meter while distinguishing approach, rest and withdrawal. Repeated recorded trials retain the zero reading at rest rather than discarding it as an uninteresting failure.

items.label: Ring transient record
items.description: The second winding gives a brief response at connection and disconnection, not a sustained response while the first current stays steady. Neither winding has to move. Faraday’s surviving 1831 ring anchors this reconstructed comparison.

items.label: Change-not-presence argument
items.description: The moving magnet and the stationary ring support the same distinction: changing magnetic linkage, not mere magnetic presence, induces the response. Mechanical motion is one way to obtain the change, not a requirement in every arrangement.

items.label: Field-and-induction model
items.description: The model connects a spatial magnetic pattern to a changing linkage through a coil. It explains the contrasting observations without claiming that the compass map alone proves induction, or that one diagram supplies a complete electromagnetic theory.

items.label: Explained generator exhibit
items.description: The handle keeps changing magnetic linkage through the generator’s coil, and the recorded lamp responds while it turns. The handle supplies mechanical energy: the magnet is not a fuel. The exhibit now connects an everyday generator with the earlier contrast between steady presence and change.

stages.title: Why does the needle move only then?
stages.speaker: Electricity-gallery curator
stages.motivation: The generator’s lamp looks like a trick. Prepare an exhibit that explains it from the compass, coil and ring observations, keeping the quiet intervals as carefully as the needle movements.
stages.completionText: Visitors can now follow the evidence from a turning compass to a generator’s lamp—and see why a motionless magnet beside a motionless coil is not a perpetual source of electricity. These reconstructed comparisons join distinct investigations; they do not turn a shared, contested history into one inventor’s inevitable ladder.

area.label: An electricity and magnetism teaching collection
area.travelText: We retrieve our experimental protocol from the archive and enter a gallery of recorded demonstrations and enclosed educational apparatus. Other collections stay where we left them.

caches.label: Compass, coil and ring collection
caches.narrative: Recovered educational displays and labeled observation records sit beside a replica of Faraday’s induction ring. These are interpretive exhibits, not instructions for constructing or powering apparatus.

sources.title: Ørsted compass needle, 1828 — Science Museum Group
sources.note: A surviving demonstration instrument, not a claim about a single dramatic discovery moment.

sources.title: Oersted’s experiment — Institute of Physics
sources.note: Supports opposite compass directions above and below a current-carrying wire. Construction and power-supply instructions deliberately excluded.

sources.title: Michael Faraday’s ring-coil apparatus — Royal Institution
sources.note: August 1831 apparatus and brief induced current in the other coil; object evidence anchors the reconstruction.

sources.title: Electromagnetism — Institute of Physics
sources.note: Field representation and induction effects: magnet/coil movement, and changing field without mechanical movement. Modern teaching interpretation, not a transcript of 1831 reasoning.

sources.title: Generators — Institute of Physics
sources.note: Changing magnetic linkage in a generator; energy transferred through a mechanical pathway. No construction instructions reproduced.

sources.title: Induced Emf and Magnetic Flux — OpenStax College Physics
sources.note: Figures 23.3–23.4 explicitly compare switch transients and opposite magnet motions with the stationary null.

sources.title: Magnetic Fields and Lines — OpenStax University Physics
sources.note: Compass direction defines a field-line direction; lines are representations.

notes: The standalone harness supplies the already-earned experimental-protocol. Integration must retrieve the existing kind instead; do not add it to the chapter cache.
All player pre-use text lives in item descriptions and stage/cache narrative; discovery text lives in recipe and result descriptions.
No voltages, apparatus construction steps, safety guarantees, fictitious quotations, or new engine mechanics.
No calibration kind is reused: a weight-calibrated scale cannot calibrate this needle meter. Qualitative direction/zero observations do not pretend to be a numerical current measurement.
